page_title: Store-to-Load Forwarding and Memory Disambiguation in x86 Processors

sources.entry: Store-to-Load Forwarding and Memory Disambiguation in x86 Processors - Measures which store and load size and offset pairs forward or stall, and which cores predict memory dependences.

summary.title: Store-to-Load Forwarding and Memory Disambiguation in x86 Processors
summary.one_liner: Learn how x86 CPUs forward store data to dependent loads and predict memory dependences, with measured latencies and forwarding-success charts for nine Intel and AMD microarchitectures.
takeaways: Store-to-load forwarding needs the CPU to match loads against uncommitted stores in the store queue, and fails for partial overlaps on most x86 designs.
Memory dependence speculation lets loads run before earlier store addresses are known, but mispredictions can be costly; Bulldozer and Piledriver appear to lack a dependence predictor.
Two microbenchmarks (fast address vs. fast data) separate forwarding latency from the cost of speculating on dependences.
Forwarding behaviour varies by offset and cache-line or 16-byte boundary crossings, which the author charts for all 64x64 offset pairs.
summary.summary: The article explains why store queues make load-store dependencies hard to track in out-of-order x86 CPUs, and describes store-to-load forwarding and memory dependence speculation. Henry Wong builds two microbenchmarks: a "fast address" version where store addresses resolve early, and a "fast data" version where late-resolving addresses force speculation. He measures results on nine Intel and AMD microarchitectures and plots forwarding latency across all 4,096 combinations of 8-byte store and 4-byte load offsets within 64-byte lines. The author concludes that recent Intel chips forward well but pay a high penalty for predicted-dependent loads, and that AMD Bulldozer and Piledriver likely mispredict every time, incurring roughly 30 to 50 cycle flushes.
